newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Africa urged to tackle corruption to get finance.
newsitem.headline: Africa urged to tackle corruption to get finance.

text.p: Southern African governments need to cut bribery and corruption to create an attractive environment for investment in their proposed regional Beira Development Corridor, a leading banker said on Tuesday.

James de la Fargue, a corporate finance manager with the Merchant Bank of Central Africa, told a two-day conference that security and exchange control concerns were also key constraints to attracting capital to turn Mozambique's Beira sea route into a regional development corridor.
"Control of bribery and corruption is a major concern. Key financial constraints are security, functionality and exchange control understanding...," de la Fargue said.

"The way forward lies with central governments getting together and creating the right kind of conducive environment that will benefit investment in the corridor," he told about 350 leading industrialists, top government officials and potential international investors.

Officials of the Beira Corridor Group, which organised the conference, said they had no estimate yet on the amount of initial capital needed to expand the Beira Corridor's road, port and rail network and transform it into a development corridor.

But the group's managing director, David Zausmer, and other speakers at the meeting stressed the region's private sector was crucial to securing the capital as southern African governments faced mounting budgetary constraints and dwindling donor aid.

De la Fargue listed among the investment security constraints; questions on tenure of land and buildings, legal system, guarantees, ability to remit and disinvest from the corridor whose catchment area includes Botswana, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia, Zaire and Zimbabwe.
But he said these could be overcome through clarification of rules governing the corridor and support from central banks through clear exchange controls on investments.

De la Fargue said the timing of the Beira Development Corridor was right, with the region enjoying a sustained period of peace after years of civil strife and destabilisation from South Africa's former apartheid rulers.

"The need for a regional approach is clear...Current manufacturing capacities cannot be filled by local demand alone and new investments in capacity or upgrading can be done with a wider end market; the interest rate regime is now making new investment and expansion a real alternative," he said.
He said Beira would also offer a cheaper route than South Africa for most regional companies.
